exemplar.title: What strong work looks like
exemplar.intro: Here is how a strong baker explains a different shop — a juice stand splitting big jugs into small cups — so you can see the moves, not the answers.

traits.trait: Names the operation and the reciprocal
traits.sample: To split 3/4 gallon of lemonade into 1/8-gallon cups, I divided by 1/8, which is the same as multiplying by the reciprocal, 8.
traits.why: Naming fraction division and the reciprocal step is exactly what the top rubric row asks for.

traits.sample: The quotient was 6, so I can pour exactly 6 full cups from that jug — the answer counts servings, not gallons.
traits.why: Explaining what the quotient represents shows the model is understood, not just computed.

traits.sample: When I switched to smaller 1/16-gallon tasting cups, I got 12 servings, because a smaller divisor always gives a bigger quotient.
traits.why: Stating the divisor-quotient relationship in words is the expert move the peer-analysis row rewards.

traits.sample: Six cups from 3/4 gallon makes sense, because each cup is tiny and 8 cups would fill a whole gallon.
traits.why: A quick sense-check proves the answer was verified against the real situation.
